title: Which Tasks Should Be Learned Together in Multi-task Learning?
venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
problem_statement: In multi-task learning, jointly training all tasks in a single neural network frequently causes negative transfer due to gradient interference and competing task objectives, resulting in accuracy inferior to standalone single-task models; identifying which tasks cooperate or compete to determine optimal task-to-network groupings under inference time budgets remains an open computational challenge.
domain: Computer Vision, Deep Multi-Task Learning, Task Compatibility and Task Grouping under Inference Time Constraints
theoretical_framework: Hard parameter sharing multi-task learning; task cooperation versus task competition dynamics; negative transfer in deep neural representations; combinatorial optimization (Branch-and-Bound reduction from Set Cover) for optimal task subset assignment under computational budgets.
methodology: The authors develop a computational framework to determine optimal task groupings for multi-task learning under inference time budgets: (1) Formulate task grouping as minimizing total loss over a task set T subject to combined inference time cost <= b; (2) Exhaustively train candidate networks across all 2^|T| - 1 possible task subsets (evaluating 36 candidate architectures across full-size and half-size encoders); (3) Solve the NP-hard network selection problem via branch-and-bound optimization; (4) Propose two time-saving approximation strategies: Early Stopping Approximation (ESA), which predicts final performance using validation loss after 20% training (yielding ~20x speedup), and Higher Order Approximation (HOA), which estimates performance on 3+ tasks by linearly averaging first-order pairwise task performances (~45% speedup). Evaluated across four controlled experimental settings varying network capacity (standard vs. high-capacity Xception), dataset size (full vs. 5% subset / 200k examples), and task distributions (Task Set 1: semantic segmentation, depth, normals, keypoints, edges; Task Set 2: autoencoding, normals, occlusion edges, reshading, principal curvature).
datasets: Taskonomy Dataset: Subset of indoor scene images evaluated across four experimental settings. Standard training uses 4 million images across non-overlapping buildings; Setting 3 uses a reduced subset of 199,498 training images (420 images from each training building).
Task Set 1: Semantic Segmentation, Surface Normal Prediction, Depth Estimation, Keypoint Detection, 2D Edge Detection.
Task Set 2: Autoencoder, Surface Normal Prediction, Occlusion Edges, Reshading, Principal Curvature.

metrics: Total Multi-Task Loss under inference time budget (Single Network Time, SNT, evaluated from 1 SNT to 5 SNT in 0.5 SNT increments)
Pairwise Multi-Task Affinity (% relative performance gain or drop relative to standalone training)
Pearson correlation (r) across training settings and against transfer affinities
baselines: Single-Task Networks (independent dedicated networks per task evaluated at full and half capacity)
All-in-One Multi-Task Network (single shared network training all tasks simultaneously)
Random Task Grouping (average of 1 million valid random task assignments)
Pessimal Task Grouping (worst-case feasible task assignment)

key_findings: Training all tasks in a single large multi-task network is often suboptimal; assigning compatible cooperating tasks to a few smaller networks consistently outperforms both all-in-one MTL and isolated single-task models across all computational budgets.

Multi-task task affinities do not correlate with transfer learning task affinities (e.g., Pearson r = -0.12 with Taskonomy), demonstrating that transfer relationships cannot predict joint multi-task training compatibility.
Multi-task affinities are highly sensitive to network capacity and dataset size; tasks that compete under low capacity or low data often cooperate effectively when encoder capacity is increased.
More functionally similar tasks do not necessarily train well together (e.g., depth and surface normals show low multi-task affinity despite strong geometric relatedness).

Adding an auxiliary task (such as Surface Normals) can improve performance on primary outputs even when the auxiliary task itself suffers performance degradation, functioning as beneficial loss guidance.

The Higher Order Approximation (HOA) accurately estimates higher-order task combinations from pairwise networks, achieving performance close to the exact combinatorial optimum while saving 45% training computation.
scope_and_delimitations: Empirical evaluation is delimited to indoor computer vision tasks on the Taskonomy benchmark across 5-task dictionaries.
Architectures are delimited to convolutional encoder-decoder backbones (standard convolutional networks and Xception) using hard parameter sharing.

Multi-task training uses uniform loss weighting by default, with comparative baselines delimited to GradNorm and Sener & Koltun (2018) without testing recent gradient surgery methods (PCGrad, CAGrad).

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: However, because we had five tasks, more than half of the candidate set was fully trained for this approximation. The Early Stopping Approximation was usually competitive, but the solutions tended to be worse than optimal. In principle, one could stop after training on more of the data, likely resulting in better results. We could not test ESA with other data amounts because our adaptive learning rates resulted in networks that were no longer comparable after being trained on more data.
limitations.summary: Multi-task affinities are not invariant and depend heavily on network capacity, dataset volume, and training hyperparameters; the combinatorial search over candidate networks requires substantial training computation that scales exponentially without approximations; and Early Stopping Approximation is constrained by adaptive learning rate schedules.

generalizability_gap: The task grouping framework was evaluated exclusively on static computer vision dense prediction tasks in indoor environments; task compatibility dynamics and grouping behavior remain untested on natural language processing tasks, code-switched text, audio, or mixed-granularity sequence labeling and classification architectures.
methodological_gap: The framework assumes uniform task loss weighting during candidate network training and does not integrate modern gradient surgery algorithms (such as PCGrad, CAGrad, or Nash-MTL) to arbitrate gradient conflicts within task groups; additionally, the approach does not consider soft parameter sharing or modular routing.
future_work: Integrating candidate networks trained with diverse architectures, adaptive loss weighting, and dynamic gradient balancing algorithms into the grouping search.
Exploring ensemble predictions when multiple networks in a solution solve the same task.
Extending task compatibility estimation to large task sets using scalable graph-based clustering or task embedding techniques.
